## Introduction

An imputation model is usually fitted and used on the same data. In
prediction, the situation is different. We fit the imputation model once
on training data, and later apply it to new cases, for example new
patients for whom we want a prediction. The imputation model for the new
cases should be the one fitted on the training data. It should not change
because new cases come in.

`mice.mids()` does this with the argument `newdata`. It adds the new
cases to a `mids` object, imputes their missing values with the trained
imputation model, and returns the imputations for the new cases. The new
cases do not influence the imputation model.

This vignette shows how to use `newdata`, which imputation methods
`mice.mids()` uses for the new cases, and what to watch out for. See
@vanbuuren-2018-1 for multiple imputation in general.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(mice)
```

## Basic use

We use the first 20 rows of `nhanes` as training data, and the last 5
rows as new data.

```{r}
train <- nhanes[1:20, ]
newdata <- nhanes[21:25, ]
newdata
```

First, we fit the imputation model on the training data:

```{r}
imp <- mice(train, m = 5, seed = 1, print = FALSE)
```

Then we pass the new cases to `mice.mids()`:

```{r}
imp.new <- mice.mids(imp, newdata = newdata, maxit = 5, print = FALSE)
complete(imp.new, 1)
```

The result is an ordinary `mids` object with only the new cases. Methods
like `complete()` and `with()` work as usual. Internally, `mice.mids()`
appends the new cases to the training data and runs `maxit` more
iterations of the Gibbs sampler. The new cases are marked by the `ignore`
argument of `mice()`. Their values are imputed, but not used to fit the
imputation models.

The default of `maxit` in `mice.mids()` is 1, which is meant for adding
an iteration to an existing solution. For new data, use a few more
iterations, so that the imputations of the new cases can converge.

## The methods come from the trained model

`mice.mids()` imputes the new cases with the imputation methods of the
trained model, and does not choose them anew for `newdata`:

```{r}
imp$method
imp.new$method
```

This holds since mice 3.19.8. Training and deployment then use the same
imputation model. Earlier versions chose the methods again for
`newdata`, which could give a different model.

## Variables that were complete in the training data

`mice()` gives a variable without missing values the method `""`. In
the training data, `age` is complete:

```{r}
imp$method["age"]
```

The new cases may still have a missing value in such a variable. Below,
`age` is missing for one new case:

```{r}
newdata2 <- newdata
newdata2[2, "age"] <- NA
```

`mice.mids()` then assigns the default method for the type of the
variable, here `pmm`, and says so in a message:

```{r}
imp.new2 <- mice.mids(imp, newdata = newdata2, maxit = 5, print = FALSE)
imp.new2$method
complete(imp.new2, 1)
```

The predictors of `age` come from the `predictorMatrix` of the trained
model. The model for `age` is fitted on the training data, where `age`
is observed.

For a factor, the default method is `logreg`, `polyreg` or `polr`,
depending on the number of levels and whether the factor is ordered, in
the same way as in `make.method()`.

Without this rule, the missing `age` would stay `NA`. Because `age` is a
predictor of the other variables, the `NA` could then also stop the
imputation of these variables for the same case. mice 3.19.8 to 3.19.16
left such values `NA` without a warning.

## Leaving a variable unimputed

Sometimes we do not want to impute a variable in the new data. Set its
method to `""` in the trained model. Below, `bmi` is not imputed:

```{r}
imp0 <- imp
imp0$method["bmi"] <- ""
```

A missing `bmi` then stays `NA`. Because `bmi` is a predictor of the
other variables, also remove it as a predictor. Otherwise, the `NA` in
`bmi` stops the imputation of the other variables for the same case:

```{r}
imp0$predictorMatrix[, "bmi"] <- 0
imp.new0 <- mice.mids(imp0, newdata = newdata, maxit = 5, print = FALSE)
imp.new0$method
complete(imp.new0, 1)
```

`mice.mids()` keeps a method `""` that you set for a variable with
missing values in the training data, here `bmi`. It only assigns a
method to a variable that was complete in the training data.

## Models specified by `formulas` or `blocks`

With `formulas` or `blocks`, the imputation model need not include all
variables. Below, `age` has no formula:

```{r}
imp.f <- mice(
  train,
  formulas = list(
    bmi = bmi ~ age + chl,
    hyp = hyp ~ age,
    chl = chl ~ age + bmi
  ),
  m = 5, seed = 1, print = FALSE
)
imp.f$method
```

A variable outside the blocks has no imputation model, so a missing
value in the new data stays `NA`:

```{r}
imp.newf <- mice.mids(imp.f, newdata = newdata2, maxit = 5, print = FALSE)
complete(imp.newf, 1)
```

Add a formula for such a variable to the training model if it should
be imputed in new data.

## Things to watch out for

- **The new data need the same variables.** `newdata` must have the
  same columns as the training data, with the same types. Factors should
  also have the same levels. `mice.mids()` does not check this, and a
  different set of levels can give a confusing warning or wrong
  imputations.
- **Setting a factor value to `NA`.** In R, `newdata$age <- NA`
  replaces the whole column by a logical `NA`, so a factor is no longer a
  factor. Use `newdata[i, "age"] <- NA` to keep the type.
- **Reproducibility.** `mice.mids()` continues from the random number
  state stored in the trained model. Two calls with the same object and
  the same `newdata` give the same imputations.
- **The imputations of the training data are not returned.** If you
  need them, use the `mids` object of the training data.
